subject: Hierarchical model & cross validation in stan

messages.author: b17f4d0880547804
messages.subject: Hierarchical model & cross validation in stan
parts:
Hi all,
I've been searching through this forum and through the manual in how I can set up cross validation in stan.
But unfortunately I haven't been able to find much besides approximations using WAIC etc.

Below is my attempt at cross validation and how I plan summarise the model fit to the data. The model works fine and converges in a few hundred iterations. Any feedback would be welcome.

The approach I've taken is first to break up the data into 10 folds. I then hold 1 fold out and use the 9/10ths to fit the data.
Below outlines how I'm attempting to do cross validation for a single fit/held out combination, with the plan to repeat this 10 times, each with a different fold held out (i.e. so all folds are held out once). 

In the data chunk I first declare the fitted and held out (tilde) data variables. 

data {
  // Training data
  int<lower=1> n_obs;
  int<lower=1> n_spp;
  int<lower=1> spp[n_obs];
  int<lower=1> n_census;
  int<lower=1> census[n_obs];
  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[n_obs];
  vector[n_obs] census_length;
  vector[n_obs] growth_dt;
  vector[n_spp] log_rho_c;
  
  // Held out data
  int<lower=1> n_obs_tilde;
  int<lower=1> n_spp_tilde;
  int<lower=1> spp_tilde[n_obs_tilde];
  int<lower=1> census_tilde[n_obs_tilde];
  int<lower=0, upper=1> y_tilde[n_obs_tilde];
  vector[n_obs_tilde] census_length_tilde;
  vector[n_obs_tilde] growth_dt_tilde;
  vector[n_spp_tilde] log_rho_c_tilde;
}


I then fit the model as normal. 
A few notes here: First I use the increment_log_prob as opposed to the faster parameterisation using the bernoulli function because it reduces some arithmetic instabilities associated with the model and the inv_cloglog. I also overwrite intermediate steps (e.g. a_log) in the model chunk as I am not interested in these objects and it seems to reduce the RAM usage and overall output size - which is important when running many models in parallel at once using a large dataset (>160,000 observations). Lastly, most of the priors are informative - that is they have been parameterised based on other published data.

parameters { 
  
    real a0_raw[n_spp];
    real a0_mu;
    real<lower=0> a0_sigma;
    
    real a1_raw[n_census];
    real a1_mu;
    real<lower=0> a1_sigma;
    
    real b0_raw[n_spp];
    real b0_mu;  
    real<lower=0> b0_sigma;
    
    real b1_raw[n_census];
    real b1_mu;  
    real<lower=0> b1_sigma;
    
    real c0_raw[n_spp];
    real c0_mu;  
    real<lower=0> c0_sigma;
    
    real c1_raw[n_census];
    real c1_mu;  
    real<lower=0> c1_sigma;
    
    real a2;
    real b2;
    real c2;
}

transformed parameters {
    real a0[n_spp];
    real a1[n_census];

    real b0[n_spp];
    real b1[n_census];

    real c0[n_spp];
    real c1[n_census];

for (s in 1:n_spp) {
a0[s] <- a0_raw[s] * a0_sigma + a0_mu;
b0[s] <- b0_raw[s] * b0_sigma + b0_mu;
c0[s] <- c0_raw[s] * c0_sigma + c0_mu;
}

for (t in 1:n_census) {
a1[t] <- a1_raw[t] * a1_sigma + a1_mu;
b1[t] <- b1_raw[t] * b1_sigma + b1_mu;
c1[t] <- c1_raw[t] * c1_sigma + c1_mu;
}
}
model {
    real a_log;
    real b_log;
    real c_log;
    real cumulative_hazard;

for (s in 1:n_spp) {
a0_raw[s] ~ normal(0,1);
b0_raw[s] ~ normal(0,1);
c0_raw[s] ~ normal(0,1);
}

for (t in 1:n_census) {
a1_raw[t] ~ normal(0,1);
b1_raw[t] ~ normal(0,1);
c1_raw[t] ~ normal(0,1);
}

for (i in 1:n_obs) {
a_log <- a0[spp[i]] + a1[census[i]] + a2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
b_log <- b0[spp[i]] + b1[census[i]] + b2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
c_log <- c0[spp[i]] + c1[census[i]] + c2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];

cumulative_hazard <- -census_length[i] * (exp(a_log - exp(b_log) * growth_dt[i]) + exp(c_log));

if (y[i] == 0) {
increment_log_prob(cumulative_hazard);
} else {
increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard));
}
}

//PRIORS

a0_mu ~ normal(-0.87, 1);
a0_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
b0_mu ~ normal(5, 10); 
b0_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
c0_mu ~ normal(-4.42, 0.17);
c0_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
a1_mu  ~ normal(0, 0.1); 
a1_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
b1_mu  ~ normal(0, 0.1);
b1_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
c1_mu  ~ normal(0, 0.1);
c1_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

a2 ~ normal(0, 5); 
b2 ~ normal(0, 5);
c2 ~ normal(0, 5);
 }

Now I know that by not specifying the cumulative_hazard in the transformed parameters chunk means I cannot call it in the generated quantities chunk... which means I've created some extra work for myself. But again this was done to reduce RAM usage and output size.

Next I want to extract the log likelihood for both the fitted data and for the holdout data (tilde). This is because I'm interested in both how the model fit and how well it predicts.
To do this I use the generated quantities chunk. Again I overwrite intermediate steps for the same reason as above. I know I can get rid of some of these intermediate steps, but I've kept them for clarity. 

generated quantities {
      real a_log_fit;
      real b_log_fit;
      real c_log_fit;
      real cumulative_hazard_fit;
      real log_lik_fit;
      real log_lik_fit_total;
      real a_log_tilde;
      real b_log_tilde;
      real c_log_tilde;
      real cumulative_hazard_tilde;
      real log_lik_tilde;
      real log_lik_tilde_total;
      real log_like_fit_prior;
      log_lik_fit_total <- 0;
      log_lik_tilde_total <- 0;
      lp_spprior <- 0;
      lp_cenprior <- 0;
      
      
      // log likelihood for fitted model
      for (i in 1:n_obs) {
        a_log_fit <- a0[spp[i]] + a1[census[i]] + a2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
        b_log_fit <- b0[spp[i]] + b1[census[i]] + b2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
        c_log_fit <- c0[spp[i]] + c1[census[i]] + c2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
        cumulative_hazard_fit <- -census_length[i] * (exp(a_log_fit - exp(b_log_fit) * growth_dt[i]) + exp(c_log_fit));

        if (y[i] == 0) {
          log_lik_fit <- cumulative_hazard_fit;
        }
        else {
          log_lik_fit <- log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard_fit);
        }
        log_lik_fit_total <- log_lik_fit_total + log_lik_fit;
      }
      
      // log likelihood for held out data
      for (i in 1:n_obs_tilde) {
        a_log_tilde <- a0[spp_tilde[i]] + a1[census_tilde[i]] + a2 * log_rho_c_tilde[spp_tilde[i]];
        b_log_tilde <- b0[spp_tilde[i]] + b1[census_tilde[i]] + b2 * log_rho_c_tilde[spp_tilde[i]];
        c_log_tilde <- c0[spp_tilde[i]] + c1[census_tilde[i]] + c2 * log_rho_c_tilde[spp_tilde[i]];
        
        cumulative_hazard_tilde <- -census_length_tilde[i] * (exp(a_log_tilde - exp(b_log_tilde) * growth_dt_tilde[i]) + exp(c_log_tilde));
        
        if (y_tilde[i] == 0) {
          log_lik_tilde <- cumulative_hazard_tilde;
          } 
        else {
          log_lik_tilde <- log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard_tilde);
          }
        log_lik_tilde_total <- log_lik_tilde_total + log_lik_tilde;
      }
                            
}


If what I have done is correct, stan should calculate the summed log likelihood of both the fitted data (log_lik_fit_total) and the heldout data (log_li_tilde_total).
Which when ran across all heldout combinations gives me 10 log likelihoods. I can then use some summary statistic (e.g. mean or median) or even plot the distribution of these log likelihoods as a way of comparing the fit or predictive fit relative to other cross validated models (e.g. the same model, same priors, but with a different measure of growth_dt), or in the case of nested models where a predictor (e.g. a2,b2,c2) is left out, using a log ratio approach.


Side notes (potentially stupid questions): 
My understanding is that stan's lp__ is the sum of the log likelihood of the model + log probability of the priors - constants. i.e. The log posterior - constants.
How could this, or the standard log posterior be calculated in the generated quantities as a way of checking my calculations of the log likelihoods are correct? Or is this just a stupid nonsensical thing to do?

Also, I've seen it mentioned many times that lp__ should not be used in model comparison. But what if the model is structurally the same, with the same priors and the only difference is one of the predictors (e.g. growth_dt in my model) is changed with a different way of calculating growth_dt? If the prior probability remains the same, can't lp__ be used to compare models by looking at absolute differences?

 Cheers
James

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical model & cross validation in stan
parts: In addition to what you listed, lp__ also includes Jacobian adjustments for bounded parameters (which are sampled on the unconstrained scale, remember). So whatever you calculate "manually" will be different from lp__ (even if you take account of the constants that are dropped), unless there are no constrained parameters in your model (which is not the case for you, as the "sigma"-parameters are constrained to be positive).

10-fold-CV is fine and your code looks like same as in the above mentioned paper, except that you sum the terms (see below). You could probably also use leave-one-out cross-validation as described in
in the above mentioned paper.
If what I have done is correct, stan should calculate the summed log likelihood of both the fitted data (log_lik_fit_total) and the heldout data (log_li_tilde_total).

I would usually recommend not to sum log_lik's, but return log_lik for each test observation and combine test observation log_liks outside of Stan, and use values to look at outliers and compute, e.g., variance of the CV estimate. But maybe you want to use sums to save memory?

Which when ran across all heldout combinations gives me 10 log likelihoods. I can then use some summary statistic (e.g. mean or median) or even plot the distribution of these log likelihoods as a way of comparing the fit or predictive fit relative to other cross validated models (e.g. the same model, same priors, but with a different measure of growth_dt), or in the case of nested models where a predictor (e.g. a2,b2,c2) is left out, using a log ratio approach.
Yes. You can also compute standard errors as described in the above mentioned paper.

Side notes (potentially stupid questions): 
My understanding is that stan's lp__ is the sum of the log likelihood of the model + log probability of the priors - constants. i.e. The log posterior - constants.
How could this, or the standard log posterior be calculated in the generated quantities as a way of checking my calculations of the log likelihoods are correct? Or is this just a stupid nonsensical thing to do?
This was answered by Luc.

Also, I've seen it mentioned many times that lp__ should not be used in model comparison. But what if the model is structurally the same, with the same priors and the only difference is one of the predictors (e.g. growth_dt in my model) is changed with a different way of calculating growth_dt? If the prior probability remains the same, can't lp__ be used to compare models by looking at absolute differences?

Even then it would not be a good estimate for the future predictive performance.
 
Aki

Aki, I actually saw your paper and used it as a basis for how I constructed my model. The only reason I'm not monitoring the log lik for each observation is that it chews through a lot of RAM and makes the output file 4 times as big. Which isn't a problem if its just a single model I'm running. But I need to run 40 model variants, each with the 10 kfold cross validation.
Also because the models take quiet some time to run... I'm not sure actually doing LOO would be efficient here (i'm working with close to 200,000 observations).

I'm now playing around with altering the stepsize and adapt_delta to see if I can get any extra computational efficiency - more out of interest then neccessity.

My question is whether I can simply run the model for 50 iterations (i.e. not converged) to test how altering stepsize (i.e. 0.01, 0.0001) and/or adapt_delta (i.e. 0.9, 0.99) influences the speed of the warm up and the tree depth and n_divergence. messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchical model & cross validation in stan
parts:
> On May 26, 2015, at 8:12 AM, James Camac <james...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Luc and Aki,
> That makes a lot of sense re: lp__ and why I couldn't replicate it in the generated quantities.
>
> Aki, I actually saw your paper and used it as a basis for how I constructed my model. The only reason I'm not monitoring the log lik for each observation is that it chews through a lot of RAM and makes the output file 4 times as big. Which isn't a problem if its just a single model I'm running. But I need to run 40 model variants, each with the 10 kfold cross validation.
> Also because the models take quiet some time to run... I'm not sure actually doing LOO would be efficient here (i'm working with close to 200,000 observations).
>
> I'm now playing around with altering the stepsize and adapt_delta to see if I can get any extra computational efficiency - more out of interest then neccessity.

What you want to do is test that you get the same result with smaller
stepsizes. That'll make sure the step size isn't bounding you out of tails
you care about in meaningful ways.

> My question is whether I can simply run the model for 50 iterations (i.e. not converged) to test how altering stepsize (i.e. 0.01, 0.0001) and/or adapt_delta (i.e. 0.9, 0.99) influences the speed of the warm up and the tree depth and n_divergence. It seems that when I reduce the stepsize i'm getting more n_divergence. The other weird thing that happens when I alter these settings is that as soon as the model finishes adapting and starts sampling the tree depth jumps up the the maximum... Is this simply because I haven't allowed enough iterations in warm up?

There's a final step size warmup with the final mass matrix, so that's
probably getting shrunk. If you ran warmup longer, you'd see the same
increase in tree depth.

If the model runs into max tree depth, you either want to reparameterize
or up the tree depth so you don't devolve to a random walk.
> In other words... to really see the effect of these settings should I be running the model for what I usually do with this model - 2000 iterations where it generally stabilizes by ~1000 mark.

Yes.

- Bob

    for (i in 1:n_obs) {

log_alpha_fit <- log_a0[spp[i]] + log_a1[census[i]] + log_a2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
      log_beta_fit <- log_b0[spp[i]] + log_b1[census[i]] + log_b2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
      log_gamma_fit <- log_c0[spp[i]] + log_c1[census[i]] + log_c2 * log_rho_c[spp[i]];
      
      cumulative_hazard_fit <- -census_length[i] * (exp(log_alpha_fit - exp(log_beta_fit) * growth_dt[i]) + exp(log_gamma_fit));

if (y[i] == 0) {
        log_lik_fit <- cumulative_hazard_fit;
      }
      else {
        log_lik_fit <- log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard_fit);
      }
sum_log_lik_fit <- sum_log_lik_fit + log_lik_fit;

}
    
    // log likelihood for held out data

for (j in 1:n_obs_heldout) {
      log_alpha_heldout <- log_a0[spp_heldout[j]] + log_a1[census_heldout[j]] + log_a2 * log_rho_c_heldout[spp_heldout[j]];
      log_beta_heldout <- log_b0[spp_heldout[j]] + log_b1[census_heldout[j]] + log_b2 * log_rho_c_heldout[spp_heldout[j]];
      log_gamma_heldout <- log_c0[spp_heldout[j]] + log_c1[census_heldout[j]] + log_c2 * log_rho_c_heldout[spp_heldout[j]];
      
      cumulative_hazard_heldout <- -census_length_heldout[j] * (exp(log_alpha_heldout - exp(log_beta_heldout) * growth_dt_heldout[j]) + exp(log_gamma_heldout));
      
      if (y_heldout[j] == 0) {
        log_lik_heldout <- cumulative_hazard_heldout;
      } 
      else {
        log_lik_heldout <- log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard_heldout);
      }
      sum_log_lik_heldout <- sum_log_lik_heldout + log_lik_heldout;
    }
      }

So you have to make sure you assign proper values. If generated
quantities constraints get violated, the whole sampler stops because
we have no way to recover at that point.
